title: M.Jasmine Devapriya vs A.Stephen Dhanaraj on 20 September, 2017

paragraphs.text:
BEFORE THE MADURAI BENCH OF MADRAS HIGH COURT 

DATED: 20.09.2017 

CORAM 

THE HONOURABLE MR.JUSTICE G.R.SWAMINATHAN 

C.M.A.(MD).No.1772 of 2010 


M.Jasmine Devapriya ... Appellant/Respondent
Vs.

A.Stephen Dhanaraj ... Respondent/Petitioner

PRAYER : This Civil Miscellaneous Appeal is filed under Section 55 of the
Indian Divorce Act, to set aside the order passed by the learned Principal
District Judge, Tuticorin in I.D.O.P.No.165 of 2004, dated 27.08.2010.

!For Appellant : Mr.N.Dilip Kumar
^For Respondent : Mr.S.Kadarkarai 


:JUDGMENT

This Appeal is at the instance of the wife. The respondent
herein filed I.D.O.P.No.165 of 2004 on the file of the learned Principal
District Judge, Tuticorin on 05.07.2004, seeking dissolution of his marriage
with the appellant herein that was solemnised on 21.01.2004. The said
Original Petition was filed under Section 10 (1) (iv) of the Indian Divorce
Act, 1969.

2. According to the pleadings set out in the said Original
Petition, the appellant herein was suffering from leprosy and that without
disclosing the existence of the said disease, the appellant was given in
marriage to the respondent. The parties herein lived together for hardly few
months. The appellant left the matrimonial house on 12.05.2004. In support
of his case, he examined himself as P.W.1. He also examined his mother as
P.W.2. The marriage invitation was marked as Ex.P.1.

3. The appellant herein filed her counter controverting the
allegation made in the Original Petition. In the counter, it is specifically
mentioned in Paragraph No.6 that the appellant was suffering from Vitiligo
and that it is not leprosy. As already pointed out, the Original Petition
was filed on the ground that the appellant herein was suffering from a
virulent and incurable form of leprosy. In other words, mere suffering from
leprosy is not sufficient, it must be a virulent and incurable form of
leprosy.

4. In the present case, the appellant herein categorically
denied even suffering from leprosy. Her skin condition was known as Vitiligo.
The Vitiligo and a Virulent and incurable form of leprosy are not one and the
same. When a specific stand was taken by the appellant, it is incumbent on
the part of the respondent herein to prove this allegation through medical
evidence that the appellant was actually suffering from a kind of leprosy
referred to Section 10 (1) (iv) of the Divorce Act, 1869. The
husband/respondent herein miserably failed to discharge the burden cast on
him.

5. The appellant herein had examined herself as R.W.1. The Court
below chose to refer to her deposition and come to a conclusion that the
appellant had committed cruelty. In support of such a conclusion, the Court
below relied on the police complaint given by the appellant herein before the
Deputy Superintendent of Police, Kangeyam for getting back her articles. It
also held that the appellant herein did not cooperate to take treatment for
her skin condition.

6. Interestingly, taking back her house-hold articles, jewels,
cash etc., is construed as an act of cruelty. Be that as it may, to grant
divorce on the ground of cruelty, the appellant herein must have treated her
husband with such cruelty as to cause a reasonable apprehension in the mind
of the respondent that it would be harmful or injurious for the respondent to
live with the appellant herein. It would be useful to compare the language
in Section 13(1)(ia) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 and Section 10(1)(x) of
the Divorce Act, 1869. While, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 provides for grant of
divorce, if other party has after the solemnization of the marriage, treated
the petitioner with cruelty, Section 10 (1) (x) of the Divorce Act, 1869
speaks of a far aggravated form of cruelty.

7. In the present case, even the respondent herein did not allege
before the Court below that he felt it would be unsafe for him to live with
the appellant herein. When the respondent herein did not attempt to bring
his case within the four corners of the statutory provision as set out in
 Section 10 (1) (x) of the Divorce Act, 1869, the Court below ought not to
have undertaken the unnecessary exercise of stretching the pleadings as well
as the law to grant relief in favour of the respondent herein. The
respondent herein approached the Court with a very specific stand. It is the
case of the respondent herein that the appellant was suffering from a
virulent and incurable form of leprosy. He admittedly failed to prove his
case. The Court below ought to have simply dismissed the petition. Instead,
the divorce petition was allowed by stretching the facts and straining the
law.

8.This Court therefore sets aside the order dated 27.08.2010
made in I.D.O.P.No.165 of 2004 on the file of the Principal District Judge,
Tuticorin. This Civil Miscellaneous Appeal stands allowed. No costs.

2.The Record Keeper, 
 VR Section,
 Madurai Bench of Madras High Court,
 Madurai.
